method: Headlines from the source feed, read by Claude: summary and four beats in Blue Street's own words from each article's headline and public text; impact = which way the headline pushes each market (dir bullish/bearish/mixed, strength 1 mild, 2 clear, 3 strong). Evidence, not a call.

USD.text: The dollar sits near a one-month low, with the euro around $1.12, after hopes of an end to the Iran war pulled oil down and cut demand for safe places to park money. But US job openings and factory orders both beat forecasts on Tuesday, which backs the Federal Reserve officials who want a December rate rise, so the midterm results and Friday's jobs report decide whether the dollar steadies.

EUR.text: The euro sits near $1.12 as the dollar has weakened and oil fell, and euro-zone factories kept growing in October with costs rising fast, which keeps a December rate rise by the European Central Bank possible. The race to replace ECB President Christine Lagarde, who leaves in February, has begun, while France's shrinking economy and Germany's low gas stores going into winter are the weak spots.

GBP.text: The pound sits near $1.345 and at its strongest against the euro this year, and British factories just had their best month for output in two years with prices rising faster. Economists expect the Bank of England to lift its rate from 3.75% to 4% on Thursday, November 5, its first rise since 2023, so a hold or a split vote would likely knock the pound.

JPY.text: The Bank of Japan held its rate at 1.25% on Friday but said underlying inflation has reached its 2% goal, and one board member wanted a rise straight away, so a December hike looks likely. Monday's fall in oil helps Japan, which buys almost all its energy abroad, and Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama repeated that Tokyo will act against wild yen swings, though the yen still sits near 157.6 per dollar.

CHF.text: Swiss inflation jumped to 1.5% in October on dearer fuel, above forecasts, which makes a December rate cut by the Swiss National Bank harder to justify. The franc also gains when investors look for shelter, and while Iran peace talks sap that demand, US strikes on an Iranian island and a deadly attack on a ship off Oman show the fighting has not stopped.

CAD.text: The Bank of Canada raised its rate to 2.5% last week, its first rise in three years, and on Tuesday Governor Tiff Macklem repeated that more rises may be needed as fuel costs keep inflation near 3%. That rate support is offset by oil, Canada's main export, which has swung with every turn in the Iran peace talks, and by a stalled economy facing new US tariffs.

AUD.text: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised its rate to 4.85% on Tuesday, its fifth rise this year, but three of nine board members wanted to hold and Governor Michele Bullock said it is a good time to take stock, which reads as a pause. The Australian dollar slipped below 70 US cents, and China's move to slow the yuan's climb adds a little more weight.

NZD.text: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand surprised by keeping its rate at 2.75% on October 28 instead of raising it, so the kiwi has lost its rate support and sits near 56 US cents. Dairy prices, the country's biggest export, rose for a third auction in a row on Tuesday, a small help, but Australia's central bank also hints at a pause and China is leaning against a stronger yuan.

XAU.text: Gold fell to its lowest in a year on Friday, below $3,900 an ounce, as Federal Reserve officials talked up more rate rises and some investors sold it to cover stock losses. It bounced on Monday as oil fell but slipped again on Tuesday, because markets still put about a 74% chance on a December US rate rise.

OIL.text: Oil fell about 7% on Monday on hopes that talks would end the Iran war, bounced early Tuesday after US strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island, then slipped again to near $103 for Brent as traders bet the talks will go on. With nothing signed and world stockpiles drained, each setback can still push prices back up quickly.

items.headline: Global dairy prices rise 3% at the latest auction, a third gain in a row
items.story_title: New Zealand: dairy prices and the kiwi
items.summary: Prices at the Global Dairy Trade auction, where New Zealand's Fonterra and others sell milk products, rose 3% on Tuesday, more than expected and the third rise in a row.

beats.was: Dairy is New Zealand's biggest export, so prices at the twice-monthly Global Dairy Trade auction feed straight into farm incomes and demand for the New Zealand dollar. The kiwi has been weak since New Zealand's central bank skipped an expected rate rise on October 28.
beats.happened: The auction's price index rose 3.0%, after a 2.5% gain at the previous sale, with an average price of about $4,166 a tonne. Forecasters had expected no change, and 111 buyers won at least one bid.
beats.means: Three firm auctions in a row point to steady overseas demand for New Zealand's main product, which helps farm incomes and the country's trade balance.
beats.fx: Better dairy prices give the kiwi mild support, but on their own they rarely outweigh interest rates, and New Zealand's central bank has stepped back from raising them.

impact.why: Higher prices for New Zealand's biggest export lift its trade income.

items.watch: New Zealand's third-quarter jobs figures, out this evening US time.

items.headline: US factory orders rise 1.8% in September, beating forecasts
items.story_title: Fed: the case for a December rate rise
items.summary: Orders placed with US factories rose 1.8% in September, more than the 1.2% economists expected, led by aircraft and spending tied to artificial intelligence.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve held its main rate at 3.75% to 4.00% on October 28, but two governors wanted a rise, and markets lean toward a December hike. Monday's survey of purchasing managers showed US factory output booming in October.
beats.happened: The Commerce Department's monthly count of new factory orders rose 1.8%, and August was revised up. Aircraft orders jumped about 28%. Orders for business equipment outside aircraft and defence, a guide to company investment plans, rose 0.6%.
beats.means: Firms are still spending, especially on computers and data centres for artificial intelligence, so the economy is not slowing much. Economists warn that higher rates and squeezed household budgets could cool factories next year.
beats.fx: Solid spending gives the dollar a little support, since it adds to the case for another Fed rate rise. It lands after a strong job-openings report, so the two point the same way.

impact.why: Strong orders add a little to the case for a December Fed rate rise.

items.watch: Friday's US October jobs report.

items.headline: US job openings jump to 7.52 million in September, and more people quit
items.story_title: Fed: the case for a December rate rise
items.summary: US employers had about 7.52 million unfilled jobs at the end of September, well above the roughly 7.1 million economists expected, while layoffs fell and more workers quit to move on.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve held its main rate at 3.75% to 4.00% on October 28, but two governors voted for a rise, and markets have leaned toward a December hike. The JOLTS survey, the US Labor Department's monthly count of job openings, hires, quits and layoffs, is one of the last checks on hiring before Friday's October jobs report.
beats.happened: Openings rose by about 333,000 to 7.52 million, and August was revised up to about 7.2 million. Quits, people leaving a job by choice, rose to about 3.37 million, a sign workers feel they can find another one. Layoffs fell to about 1.64 million.
beats.means: Firms still want workers and few are cutting staff, so pay pressure is unlikely to fade fast. That supports the Fed officials who want one more rate rise to cool inflation. The survey gets fewer replies than it used to, so one month can be noisy.
beats.fx: A firmer job market gives the dollar some support, because it makes a December rate rise easier to justify. The bigger tests are tonight's midterm results and Friday's jobs report.

impact.why: More openings and fewer layoffs back the case for a December Fed rate rise.

items.watch: Friday's US October jobs report, which shows whether the hiring signal holds up.

items.headline: Oil gives back its morning bounce and falls for a second day on peace-talk hopes
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Oil turned lower in US trading on Tuesday, with Brent near $103 a barrel and US crude near $95, as hopes for US-Iran peace talks outweighed overnight US strikes on an Iranian island.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war since late February, and Iran keeps most traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for Gulf oil, shut. Oil fell about 7% on Monday on hopes of a peace deal, then rose almost 2% early Tuesday after US strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island.
beats.happened: By midday in New York the early rise had gone. Brent slipped about 1% to near $103 and US crude to near $95, a second daily fall, as traders bet the talks will carry on despite the strikes.
beats.means: The market is treating the Qeshm strikes as a one-off rather than a return to full fighting, and is pricing a better chance of a deal. Prices are still far above where they started the year, so any setback can quickly undo the drop.
beats.fx: Cheaper oil helps big energy buyers like Japan and the euro zone and eases inflation worries, while it takes some support from the Canadian dollar.

impact.why: Hopes for a peace deal win out over the overnight strikes, pulling prices down a second day.
Oil is Canada's main export, so a lower price trims support for the loonie.
Japan buys almost all its energy abroad, so cheaper oil eases the drain on the yen.

items.watch: Whether Washington replies to Iran's latest proposal, and whether Iran answers the Qeshm strikes.

items.headline: Bank of Canada's Macklem tells MPs further rate rises could be needed
items.story_title: Bank of Canada: a rate rise to fight energy-driven inflation
items.summary: Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem told a parliamentary committee the bank may need to raise rates again but will move carefully, repeating last week's message.

beats.was: The Bank of Canada raised its rate to 2.5% on October 28, its first rise since 2023, to stop high fuel prices from spreading into wider inflation. Canada's inflation has run near 3% since April.
beats.happened: Speaking to the House of Commons finance committee, Macklem said inflation could reach about 3.5% by year-end and stay at or above 3% through much of 2027. Further rises are possible, he said, but the bank will decide one meeting at a time.
beats.means: Nothing new: he repeated last week's guidance almost word for word. Markets see roughly even odds of another rise at the December 9 meeting.
beats.fx: The message keeps some rate support under the Canadian dollar, but since it was already expected, it adds little. Oil, Canada's main export, still matters more day to day.

impact.why: Keeps a December Bank of Canada rate rise possible, though already expected.

items.watch: Macklem speaks to a Senate committee on Thursday, November 5; the next rate decision is December 9.

items.headline: Strategists still see a weaker dollar ahead, but more now fear it holds up
items.story_title: US midterms: a week of elections, central banks and jobs data
items.summary: A Reuters poll of currency strategists still sees the euro climbing to about $1.16 within a year, but most of those asked think the dollar is more likely to beat their forecasts than fall short.

beats.was: The dollar has slipped to near a one-month low, with the euro around $1.12, as oil fell on hopes of an end to the Iran war. Americans vote on Tuesday in midterm elections that decide control of Congress.
beats.happened: Reuters' monthly poll of 66 forecasters put the euro at about $1.13 in three months and about $1.16 in a year, so the call for a weaker dollar stands. But 17 of 30 strategists asked a follow-up question said the dollar is more likely to come in stronger than they forecast.
beats.means: Forecasters keep their view of a slowly weaker dollar, but they are less sure of it, with US growth holding up and the Federal Reserve leaning toward another rate rise rather than cuts.
beats.fx: The poll adds little new pressure on its own. It shows the expected path for the dollar is lower, but the risks around that path tilt toward a firmer dollar.

impact.why: Forecasts still point lower, but most strategists asked see more risk of a stronger dollar.
The median forecast has the euro rising toward $1.16 over the next year.

items.watch: Midterm results overnight and Friday's US jobs report, which will show whether the dollar steadies.

items.headline: Swiss inflation jumps to 1.5% in October on fuel costs
items.story_title: Switzerland: inflation picks up on fuel costs
items.summary: Swiss prices rose 1.5% from a year earlier in October, up from 1.0% and above the 1.3% expected, almost entirely because fuel got dearer; underlying prices stayed calm.

beats.was: Swiss inflation has been very low for two years, inside the Swiss National Bank's 0-2% target, and some traders had hoped the bank would cut its rate again in December. The Iran war has pushed fuel prices sharply higher this year.
beats.happened: The Federal Statistical Office said prices rose 0.2% in the month, against no change expected, and 1.5% over the year, the highest since late 2023. Petrol, diesel and heating oil drove nearly all of it. Core inflation, which leaves out energy and fresh food, held at just 0.5%.
beats.means: Higher headline inflation makes a December rate cut by the Swiss National Bank harder to argue for. But because the rise is in fuel and not in everyday prices, the bank is unlikely to feel pushed to raise rates.
beats.fx: Supports the Swiss franc by cutting the odds of a December rate cut; the calm core reading limits how far that goes.

impact.why: A clear beat that makes a December rate cut less likely.

items.watch: The Swiss National Bank's December 10 decision, and whether fuel costs keep rising.

items.headline: US carries out 'defensive' strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island, officials say
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: US officials said American forces made limited strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, hours after President Trump played down new attacks; oil edged back up in Asia.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war since late February, and Iran keeps most traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, shut. Oil fell about 7% on Monday on hopes for a peace deal after Trump said he was not planning strikes after the US midterm elections.
beats.happened: The Wall Street Journal first reported, and a US official then confirmed, strikes on Qeshm, the biggest island in the strait. Officials called them limited and defensive, a reply to Iran firing missiles at US aircraft, and said they do not mean full fighting has restarted. Iranian state media reported several blasts on the island. Brent crude rose about 0.5% to near $105 a barrel in early Asian trade.
beats.means: Even with talks moving and both sides sounding hopeful, the two militaries are still trading fire around the strait. That keeps a risk of escalation alive and makes the market's bet on a quick deal shakier.
beats.fx: Any sign the fighting is not over adds some war premium back to oil and supports the dollar and Swiss franc as safe places to hold money, while it hurts big energy buyers like Japan.

impact.why: Fresh US-Iran fire in the strait revives the risk to Gulf supply after Monday's big drop.
Renewed war risk adds some demand for the dollar as shelter.
Investors lean on the franc when conflict risk rises.
Japan imports almost all its energy, so pricier oil weighs on it.
Canada exports oil, so a firmer oil price helps its currency.

items.watch: Whether Iran answers the Qeshm strikes, and whether the draft deal from the Qatar talks survives them.

items.headline: Tech losses weigh on world markets as Americans vote in the midterms
items.story_title: US midterms: a week of elections, central banks and jobs data
items.summary: Stock markets in Asia and Europe slipped on Tuesday as worries about AI spending hit tech shares, while Americans voted in midterm elections that decide control of Congress.

beats.was: The US holds midterm elections on Tuesday, November 3, for control of both houses of Congress and many governors' offices, halfway through President Trump's second term. The dollar had already slipped to around a one-month low on Monday as oil fell.
beats.happened: South Korea's main share index fell about 4% and Taiwan's nearly 4% as investors questioned whether heavy spending on AI data centres will pay off, and US stock futures pointed lower. Oil rose about 1.7% after US strikes on Iranian targets, and the euro edged up to about $1.12.
beats.means: The dollar is drifting rather than rising into the vote. The result shapes how much of Trump's agenda on tariffs, taxes and spending can pass in his last two years, and early counts arrive overnight.
beats.fx: Little new push for the dollar until results come in; falling tech shares add some demand for safer assets like the yen.

impact.why: A vote that decides Congress, but no result yet and the dollar is waiting.
Falling stock markets tend to bring some buying of the yen as a shelter.

items.watch: Midterm results overnight, then US job openings data and Friday's October jobs report.

items.headline: Race to replace Lagarde at the ECB begins, with nominations due Friday
items.story_title: ECB: choosing Lagarde's successor
items.summary: Euro-zone governments have until Friday, November 6, to name candidates to succeed Christine Lagarde as European Central Bank president; Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos and the Netherlands' Klaas Knot lead early betting.

beats.was: Christine Lagarde, president of the European Central Bank, said on October 29 she will leave on February 7, about nine months before her term ends. The same day the bank held its deposit rate at 2.5%.
beats.happened: Euro-zone finance ministers will review nominations on November 9, and a winner needs the backing of at least 16 of the 21 member countries. Front-runners are Pablo Hernández de Cos, head of the Bank for International Settlements and former Bank of Spain governor, and Klaas Knot, who ran the Dutch central bank for 14 years. Executive Board member Isabel Schnabel also leaves in January and chief economist Philip Lane's term ends in May, so half the bank's top board changes within five months.
beats.means: The next president will shape euro-zone rates for eight years. Knot has a record of favouring tighter policy, while Hernández de Cos is seen as more middle-of-the-road, so the choice could shift how quickly the bank raises or cuts in future. Lagarde still chairs the December and February meetings.
beats.fx: Little effect on the euro for now, since nothing changes before February, but a clear lean toward a tougher-on-inflation pick would give the euro mild support.

impact.why: A leadership change ahead, with the direction of policy depending on who wins.

items.watch: Which names governments submit by Friday, November 6, and what the finance ministers signal on November 9.

items.headline: Oil climbs back as Iran says a peace deal is still far off
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Oil rose almost 2% on Tuesday, with Brent near $106.60 a barrel, after a senior Iranian official said Tehran and Washington are far from a deal to end their war.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war for about eight months, and Iran's grip on the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane that carries much of the Gulf's oil, has kept prices high. On Monday oil fell more than 7% on hopes that talks hosted by Qatar would end the fighting.
beats.happened: A US official confirmed American forces struck Iran's Qeshm Island, inside the strait, calling it a defensive move to stop attacks on merchant ships. A senior Iranian official then said the two sides are far apart and Tehran will not accept what it sees as too much being asked of it, though parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf said Iran had sent its reply and now waits on Washington. Brent rose about $1.80 and US crude about $1.60, to near $98.
beats.means: Monday's hope that the war is ending has cooled a little, so some of the extra price for war risk is back in oil. Talks have not collapsed, which keeps a lid on the bounce for now.
beats.fx: Dearer oil helps the Canadian and Norwegian currencies and hurts big oil buyers like Japan and the euro zone; it also nudges up inflation fears, which tends to support the dollar.

impact.why: Iran says a deal is far off, putting some war risk back into prices after Monday's big fall.
Oil is Canada's main export, so a rebound gives the loonie a little help.
Japan buys almost all its energy abroad, so dearer oil weighs on the yen.

items.watch: Whether Washington answers Iran's reply, and any new attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

items.headline: Indian cargo ship hit off Oman; one sailor killed
items.story_title: Hormuz: shipping attacks and the oil supply
items.summary: An Indian-flagged cargo ship was hit by an unidentified flying object off Oman on Monday, killing one of its 14 crew; it adds to a string of attacks on ships near the Strait of Hormuz.

beats.was: Ships near the Strait of Hormuz, the channel that carries about a fifth of the world's oil, have come under repeated attack during the Iran war, including tankers hit over the weekend. Oil had just fallen sharply on hopes of peace talks.
beats.happened: India's shipping minister, Sarbananda Sonowal, said the cargo vessel AL JUSUFI was struck near the coast of Oman on November 2. One sailor died and the other 13 were rescued by Oman's coast guard. No one has said who carried out the attack.
beats.means: It was a small cargo ship, not an oil tanker, so supply is not directly hit. But a deadly attack shows the waters around Hormuz are still dangerous even as talks go on, which keeps shipping and insurance costs high.
beats.fx: Adds a little support to oil and to currencies of oil exporters, and a touch of shelter demand; small on its own.

impact.why: Another attack near Hormuz keeps supply worries alive, though no oil cargo was hit.

items.watch: Whether attacks on ships keep coming while US-Iran talks continue.

items.headline: Australia's Bullock says it is time to take stock after the rate rise; Aussie dips below 70 US cents
items.story_title: Reserve Bank of Australia: a fifth rate rise this year?
items.summary: Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Michele Bullock said after Tuesday's rate rise that it is a good moment to pause and check the data, and the Australian dollar slipped below 70 US cents.

beats.was: Earlier on Tuesday the Reserve Bank of Australia raised its rate by a quarter point to 4.85%, its fifth rise of 2026, in a six-to-three vote with three board members wanting to hold.
beats.happened: At her press conference, Governor Bullock said she does not know what the next move will be, but it is probably a good point to take stock and see whether the data match the bank's forecasts. She said the three who wanted to hold worried more about housing and rising unemployment, and that the bank is not aiming for a recession. The Australian dollar fell about 0.3% to near 69.8 US cents, around a two-week low.
beats.means: Together with the split vote, this reads as a pause after a long run of rises, though she kept the door open because inflation risks still point up. A December rise now looks less likely than before the meeting.
beats.fx: Leans on the Australian dollar, since markets see fewer rate rises ahead than they did a day ago.

impact.why: A clear hint of a pause, and the currency dropped below 70 US cents.
The kiwi tends to follow the Australian dollar.

items.watch: Australian jobs and inflation data before the December 8 meeting.

items.headline: Gold slips as US voters go to the polls
items.story_title: Gold: sliding as Fed rate-rise bets build
items.summary: Gold eased about 0.5% to near $3,927 an ounce early Tuesday, giving back part of Monday's 2% bounce from a one-year low, as markets still expect a US rate rise in December.

beats.was: Gold fell to its lowest in a year on Friday as US Federal Reserve officials talked of raising rates again, and some investors sold it to raise cash after stock market losses. It bounced more than 2% on Monday as oil fell.
beats.happened: Spot gold dipped to around $3,927 in Asian trading. Futures markets put about a 74% chance on the Fed raising rates in December, and Americans vote in midterm elections for Congress on Tuesday. One analyst said gold is still being sold to cover losses elsewhere rather than bought as a shelter.
beats.means: Gold earns no interest, so the prospect of higher US rates keeps weighing on it. Until that December rate-rise chance fades, bounces like Monday's struggle to last.
beats.fx: Mild pressure on gold; no big push for currencies.

impact.why: A small dip as a likely December US rate rise keeps weighing on gold.

items.watch: Midterm results overnight and Friday's US October jobs report, which shape the odds of a December rate rise.

items.headline: Reserve Bank of Australia raises rates to 4.85%, as widely expected
items.story_title: Reserve Bank of Australia: a fifth rate rise this year?
items.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised its rate to 4.85% on Tuesday, its fifth rise this year, but three of its nine board members wanted to hold and it gave no hint of more.

beats.was: Australian prices have kept rising fast this year, helped by fuel costs from the Iran war, and the central bank had already lifted its rate four times in 2026. Markets put the chance of another rise at close to 90%, so the move itself was no surprise.
beats.happened: The board lifted the cash rate by a quarter point to 4.85%, its highest since 2008. The vote was six to three, with three members preferring to stay at 4.60%. New forecasts show inflation above 3% for the next year and only reaching the top of the 2-3% target by late 2027, while unemployment rises more than expected. The bank said it will watch the data rather than promising further rises.
beats.means: A split board and no signal of more rises suggest this could be the last increase for now, even though inflation is expected to stay too high for longer. Governor Michele Bullock's press conference is the next clue on whether a December rise is still on the table.
beats.fx: The higher rate was already priced, so the Australian dollar gets little new lift from it; the three dissents and the open-ended wording lean against a lasting gain.

impact.why: A higher rate supports it, but the 6-3 split and no hint of more rises cut the case for further gains.
The kiwi often moves with the Australian dollar, so a cautious hike gives it little help.

items.watch: Governor Michele Bullock's press conference on whether more rises are possible, and the December 8 decision.

items.headline: China's PBOC lifts FX reserve ratio to 6%: what it means for the yuan, AUD
items.story_title: China: slowing the yuan's climb
items.summary: China's central bank will make banks hold more of their foreign-currency deposits in reserve from November 15, a step aimed at slowing the yuan's rise.

beats.was: The yuan has gained more than 5% against the dollar this year, one of Asia's best runs, and sits near a four-year high. The People's Bank of China had already been setting its daily reference rate weaker than expected, a sign it wanted the climb to slow.
beats.happened: The bank said banks must hold 6% of foreign-currency deposits in reserve, up from 4%, starting November 15. That takes dollars out of China's banking system, making them a bit scarcer and so less cheap to buy with yuan. It reverses a cut made in 2023, when Beijing was fighting a falling yuan.
beats.means: Beijing is telling markets it does not want the yuan to rise too fast, since a strong currency hurts its exporters while the economy is slowing. The direct effect on money flows is modest; the message matters more.
beats.fx: A slower-rising yuan tends to drag a little on currencies that trade as stand-ins for China, chiefly the Australian and New Zealand dollars.

impact.why: The Australian dollar often tracks the yuan, so Beijing leaning against yuan gains weighs on it.
China is New Zealand's biggest buyer, so a capped yuan gives the kiwi less support.

items.watch: Whether the yuan's daily reference rate keeps coming in weaker than expected after the change takes effect on November 15.

items.headline: Trump raises doubts about renewed attacks on Iran
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Asked on Monday whether he was weighing new strikes on Iran after Tuesday's US midterm elections, President Trump said no, and Vice President JD Vance said talks with Iran have gone well.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war since late February, and Iran has kept most traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, shut. Trump had hinted for days that strikes could resume once the midterm vote was over, which kept a risk of fresh fighting hanging over markets.
beats.happened: After a speech in Washington he billed as his closing pitch before the vote, Trump answered no when reporters asked about post-election strikes, and said he thinks Iran wants a deal and one could happen. Vance said there had been several good conversations with the Iranians and that he and Trump feel hopeful about a negotiated end. Trump repeated that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon.
beats.means: This is the clearest sign yet that the feared post-election strike window may not come, coming a day after Iran's leadership backed the talks. Nothing is agreed, though: Iran still wants the US blockade of its ports lifted first, and attacks on Gulf shipping have not stopped.
beats.fx: Less chance of new strikes takes some war premium out of oil and trims demand for the dollar and the Swiss franc as safe places to hold money, while it helps big energy buyers like Japan and the euro zone.

impact.why: Ruling out post-election strikes lowers the risk of a new hit to Gulf supply.
Lower war risk trims demand for the dollar as a safe place.
Calmer markets reduce the pull of the franc as shelter.
Japan buys almost all its energy abroad, so a softer oil price helps it.
Canada exports a lot of oil, so a lower oil price weighs on its currency.

items.watch: Whether Washington formally answers the draft deal circulating in Qatar, and whether Iran gets any move on the port blockade.

items.headline: Iran's Khamenei Gives Government Powers to Hold Talks on War
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has given the government powers to seek an end to the war with the US through talks.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war since late February, and Iran has kept the Strait of Hormuz, the sea route for about a fifth of the world's oil, mostly shut. Iranian officials have been meeting Qatari go-betweens in Doha, and President Trump had threatened new strikes after Tuesday's US midterm elections.
beats.happened: Pezeshkian, speaking through Iran's state news agency, said Iran wants a solution through dialogue and that the Supreme Leader, who has the final say in Iran, has handed the government some powers to pursue it. He did not say what those powers are. Separately, Trump reportedly told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu he is willing to give diplomacy more time.
beats.means: It is the clearest sign yet that Iran's top authority backs the talks, which makes a deal more believable. But Iran still says it will only ease Hormuz shipping and return to formal talks once the US lifts its blockade of Iranian ports, so the hardest step is untouched.
beats.fx: A likelier end to the war lowers oil and cuts demand for safe places to park money, which tends to weigh on the dollar and the Swiss franc and help energy importers such as Japan and the euro zone.

impact.why: Backing from Iran's Supreme Leader makes a deal that reopens Hormuz more believable.
Less war risk trims demand for the dollar as a safe place.
Calmer markets reduce the pull of the franc as shelter.
Japan buys almost all its energy abroad, so cheaper oil helps it.

items.watch: Whether Washington answers the draft proposal circulating in Qatar, and whether it moves on Iran's demand to lift the port blockade first.

items.headline: Oil drops 7% as Iran signals openness to peace talks
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Oil's slide deepened to about 7% by midday Monday, with Brent near $105 a barrel and US crude near $96.6, as Iran signalled it is ready to negotiate.

beats.was: Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, ended October at a six-month high because the US-Iran war has kept most tankers out of the Strait of Hormuz. Prices had already fallen in Asian and European trading on hopes for talks in Qatar.
beats.happened: By midday in New York, Brent was down about $8.50 at roughly $105 and US crude down $7.50 at about $96.6, the lowest of the day. Iran's leaders said they have authority to negotiate, and an official said a draft deal is circulating with another meeting possible. The head of Abu Dhabi's state oil company said the world has drawn close to a billion barrels from stockpiles since the war began.
beats.means: This is one of the biggest one-day drops of the war, driven by hope rather than a signed deal. Analysts warn there have been many false dawns, and with stockpiles drained, any setback could send prices back up quickly; Goldman Sachs sees $140 Brent in 2027 if Gulf output stays well below normal.
beats.fx: A lower oil bill helps Japan and the euro zone and takes support away from oil exporters such as Canada. It also eases the inflation worry that has kept talk of further US rate rises alive.

impact.why: About 7% wiped off prices in a day on hopes of a deal to reopen Hormuz.
Oil is Canada's biggest export, so a sharp fall cuts its income.
Japan imports nearly all its energy, so cheaper oil eases its trade bill.
The euro zone is a big energy buyer and gains from lower prices.

items.watch: Monday's closing prices and any fresh tanker attack near Hormuz, which could undo the drop.

items.headline: Oil Prices Fall Below $100 as Trump Signals Progress in Iran Negotiations
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: US crude dropped below $100 a barrel on Monday for the first time since October's climb, as President Trump said talks with Iran were going fine.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war since late February, and Iran has kept the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, mostly shut. Brent crude ended October at a six-month high. Iran has been talking to Qatari go-betweens about a plan to end the war.
beats.happened: US crude fell more than $4 to just under $100, and Brent dropped almost $5 to about $108.7, with later reports showing both down around 6% on the day. Trump said talks were going fine and the war could end very soon. Petrol and diesel futures fell sharply too.
beats.means: Markets are betting on a deal, not reacting to one: nothing is signed, Iran wants the US blockade of its ports lifted first, and tankers are still hitting mines near Hormuz. Goldman Sachs still sees Brent at $105 in December, so much of the war premium remains.
beats.fx: Cheaper oil helps energy buyers such as Japan and the euro zone and removes some support from oil exporters such as Canada; it also eases the inflation worry that has backed the dollar.

impact.why: Hope of a US-Iran deal is cutting the war premium fast, taking US crude under $100.
Lower oil trims Canada's export income.
Japan buys almost all its energy abroad, so a lower oil bill helps.
Falling oil eases US inflation fears and the demand for the dollar as a safe place.

items.watch: A US answer to the draft deal in Qatar, or fresh attacks on Gulf shipping, which could reverse the drop quickly.

items.headline: US ISM Manufacturing Jumps to 55.5 as Production Surges, But Price Pressures Persist
items.story_title: Fed: the case for a December rate rise
items.summary: US factories grew faster than expected in October, with output at its strongest in almost five years, while the rise in the prices they pay slowed a little.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve held its rate at 3.75% to 4% last week, but several of its officials say rates need to rise again, possibly in December. The ISM survey of factory purchasing managers is the first big US figure of each month; any reading above 50 means growth.
beats.happened: The ISM manufacturing index rose to 55.5 in October from 54.5, above the roughly 54.7 economists expected. Its output measure hit 59, the highest since November 2021. The prices-paid measure eased to 75.2 from 77.9, lower than forecast but still very high.
beats.means: A strong factory sector adds to the case that the US economy can take another rate rise. The small cooling in input prices takes a little of the urgency away, so this backs a December rise without forcing it.
beats.fx: Strong US growth supports the dollar against its rivals, but on the day it was outweighed by falling oil and calmer markets pulling money out of the dollar.

impact.why: A clear beat on factory growth backs the Fed officials who want higher rates, though cooling input prices soften it.
More chance of a US rate rise makes gold, which pays no interest, less attractive.

items.watch: Wednesday's ISM services survey and Friday's October jobs report; weak figures there would undo the boost from this beat.

items.headline: Iran's PGSA blacklists a further batch of vessels for breaching its Strait of Hormuz protocols, taking its non-compliant list to 240 ships
items.story_title: Hormuz: shipping attacks and the oil supply
items.summary: Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority, which Tehran set up in May to police the Strait of Hormuz, added another large batch of ships to its blacklist on Monday, taking it to about 240 vessels.

beats.was: Since the US-Iran war began in February, Iran has demanded that ships crossing Hormuz follow its rules, and it lists those it says broke them. Last week it warned it would act against every ship run by Sinokor, a South Korean company that carried over a third of the crude leaving the Gulf in September.
beats.happened: The authority published its biggest update yet, and the trade paper Seatrade Maritime reports the new names include many Sinokor-linked ships plus tankers tied to Kuwaiti, Saudi and Emirati state carriers. No listed ship has been reported seized or attacked since the update.
beats.means: A blacklist mostly adds cost and delay at first, as insurers, ports and fuel suppliers grow wary of named ships. It would only cut supply if Iran starts seizing or turning back listed vessels, which matters because it lands while both sides are talking about a deal.
beats.fx: It slightly raises the risk that fewer tankers get through Hormuz, which leans toward a higher oil price, helping oil sellers like Canada and weighing on big importers like Japan.

impact.why: More ships on Iran's list adds friction to the few tankers still crossing Hormuz.
Japan relies on Gulf oil, so any squeeze on tanker traffic raises its import bill.

items.watch: Any seizure, fine or turn-back of a newly listed ship, and whether insurers raise war-risk costs again.

items.headline: Market Quick Take - Markets find calm after Friday turmoil - 2 November 2026
items.story_title: Gold: sliding as Fed rate-rise bets build
items.summary: Gold bounced about 1% to near $3,915 an ounce early Monday after Friday's drop to its lowest in a year, as markets calmed after the worst US stock day since June.

beats.was: Gold fell almost 7% in October and broke below $3,900 on Friday, hit by talk of more US rate rises and by investors selling it to cover losses in technology stocks.
beats.happened: Saxo Bank's morning note shows gold up about 1% to roughly $3,915 and silver up about 2% to near $50.20 early Monday, with stock markets in Asia steadier and oil about 3% lower.
beats.means: This is a small recovery from forced selling, not a turn: the main weight on gold, the chance of a Federal Reserve rate rise in December, has not gone away.
beats.fx: A softer dollar on Monday helps gold a little; Friday's US jobs report matters most for the next big move.

impact.why: A modest bounce after a sharp fall as panic selling eased.

items.watch: Friday's October US jobs report; strong hiring would revive bets on a December Fed rate rise and pressure gold again.

items.headline: Eurozone manufacturing growth holds steady in October
items.story_title: Euro zone: growth holding up, prices still rising
items.summary: Euro-zone factories kept growing in October for a ninth month, though a bit more slowly, while their costs rose at the fastest pace since May.

beats.was: The European Central Bank hinted last week it could raise rates in December, after the euro zone grew faster than expected last quarter. A purchasing managers' index (PMI) reading above 50 means activity is growing.
beats.happened: S&P Global's final euro-zone manufacturing PMI for October came in at 52.7, down from 52.9 in September. Output grew at its slowest in four months, but exports rose at the quickest pace in over four years. Input costs climbed at the fastest rate since May and selling prices kept rising sharply. France and Italy were the only big members where factories shrank.
beats.means: Industry is holding up, helped by defence spending and firms building stock, and the rise in costs keeps pressure on the ECB to act on prices.
beats.fx: Steady factory growth with firmer prices backs the case for a December ECB hike, mildly supportive for the euro.

impact.why: Solid factory growth and rising costs keep a December ECB rate rise on the table.

items.watch: Wednesday's flash euro-zone inflation figure for October; a softer reading would cool the hike talk.

items.headline: UK manufacturing PMI rises to 52.8 in October
items.story_title: Bank of England: first rate rise since 2023?
items.summary: British factories had their best month in two years for output in October, and their selling prices rose at the fastest pace in three months, days before an expected Bank of England rate rise.

beats.was: Economists expect the Bank of England to lift its rate from 3.75% to 4% on Thursday, November 5, its first rise since 2023, because price pressures are building. A purchasing managers' index (PMI) reading above 50 means activity is growing.
beats.happened: S&P Global's UK manufacturing PMI rose to 52.8 in October from 51.9, a five-month high. Production grew at its fastest pace in 25 months and new orders picked up at home and abroad. Input costs rose at one of the sharpest rates in four years, factory prices climbed faster, and hiring stalled. Shipping detours and conflict-related disruption slowed deliveries.
beats.means: Firm demand plus rising costs fits the case for a Bank of England hike this week rather than against it.
beats.fx: Supports the pound by making a Thursday rate rise look safer.

impact.why: Stronger factory activity and faster price rises back the expected rate rise on Thursday.

items.watch: Thursday's Bank of England decision and how many policymakers vote to raise rates.

items.headline: Kazakhstan's Energy Ministry reports suspension of oil pumping via Atyrau-Samara pipeline
items.story_title: Drone strikes on Russian oil routes
items.summary: Kazakhstan stopped pumping oil through the Atyrau-Samara pipeline into Russia early Monday after drones hit a pumping hub near Samara; officials expect it to restart soon.

beats.was: Kazakhstan, a mid-sized oil producer, sends part of its crude north through the Atyrau-Samara pipeline into Russia's network for export. Drone attacks on Russian oil sites have disrupted Kazakh exports before.
beats.happened: Drones struck facilities at the Samara pumping and dispatch hub overnight, and pumping stopped at about 6 a.m. Kazakh time on Monday, November 2, according to Asel Serikpayeva, spokeswoman for Kazakhstan's Energy Ministry. Engineers are checking the damage. No volumes were given and no one was named as the attacker.
beats.means: This is a small, likely short break in supply. It barely registered on a day when hopes of ending the US-Iran war cut oil prices by about 7%, but it is another reminder that supply routes are fragile while world stockpiles are low.
beats.fx: Only a slight lift for oil and so for oil-exporting currencies such as the Canadian dollar; it matters more if the outage drags on.

impact.why: A brief halt on a secondary export route; restart expected soon.

items.watch: Whether pumping restarts within days, and any further drone strikes on oil sites in Russia.

items.headline: Iranians have left Doha talks, draft proposal for US deal being circulated, official says
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Iran's negotiators have left the Qatar-hosted talks with the US, but an official says a draft deal to end the war is now being passed around and another meeting may follow.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war since late February. Iran has kept the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, mostly shut, and the US has blockaded Iran's ports. Qatar has been carrying messages between the two sides.
beats.happened: An official briefed on the talks said Iran's team left Doha, Qatar's capital, on Sunday, not because the talks broke down, and that a draft agreement is circulating, without giving details. Esmaeil Baghaei, Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman, said there can be no final deal or reopening of Hormuz until the US blockade ends.
beats.means: This is the first sign of an actual text on the table, which supports the hope behind Monday's fall in oil. But Iran's conditions are steep, and President Trump has said he still has one or two targets in Iran, while promising no strikes before Tuesday's midterm elections.
beats.fx: Talk of a deal weighs on oil and on the dollar's shelter demand; it hurts oil sellers like Canada and helps big energy buyers like Japan and the euro zone.

impact.why: A draft deal makes a reopening of Hormuz more likely, but nothing is agreed and no details are known.
Cheaper oil would cut Canada's export income.
Japan imports almost all its energy, so lower oil eases its import bill.

items.watch: Whether a second round of talks is set, and whether the US eases its blockade; any new strike after Tuesday's vote would undo the hope.

items.headline: Dollar pulls back ahead of US midterms; bitcoin stabilises after crypto heist
items.story_title: US midterms: a week of elections, central banks and jobs data
items.summary: The dollar slipped to its weakest in a month on Monday and the euro jumped about 0.7% to near $1.123, as cheaper oil and calmer markets eased demand for the US currency.

beats.was: The dollar had been propped up by high oil prices, fear around the Iran war and Federal Reserve officials calling for higher US rates. Americans vote in midterm elections on Tuesday, November 3, and the Bank of England, the Reserve Bank of Australia and the central banks of Norway and Sweden all decide on rates this week.
beats.happened: The dollar index fell about 0.5% to roughly 101.45, a one-month low. The euro rose to about $1.123 even though Fitch had just warned it may cut France's credit rating, the pound edged up to about $1.345, and the yen held near 157.6 per dollar. Brent crude fell almost 4% on hopes the US-Iran war can be ended by talks. Bitcoin steadied near $78,000 after hackers stole $6.3 billion from the crypto exchange Binance last week, a theft the FBI blames on North Korea.
beats.means: With oil falling and fear easing, some of the shelter money that had gone into the dollar is flowing back out. Kit Juckes, head of currency strategy at Société Générale, pointed to better risk mood and lower oil as the weight on the dollar.
beats.fx: A softer dollar lifts the euro and pound most; the yen and Australian dollar barely moved ahead of their own news.

impact.why: Cheaper oil and calmer markets cut demand for the dollar as a safe place, taking it to a one-month low.
The euro had its best start to a week in a while, shrugging off the warning on France's credit rating.
A small gain against a weaker dollar ahead of Thursday's Bank of England decision.

items.watch: Tuesday's midterm results and Friday's October US jobs report; renewed fighting in the Gulf would likely send money back into the dollar.

items.headline: [PREVIEW] RBA Rate Decision Scheduled for Tuesday 3rd November 2026 at 03:30GMT
items.story_title: Reserve Bank of Australia: a fifth rate rise this year?
items.summary: Markets give about an 81% chance that the Reserve Bank of Australia raises its rate by a quarter point to 4.85% on Tuesday, alongside new inflation forecasts.

beats.was: Australia's central bank has been raising its cash rate this year to fight inflation, taking it to 4.60%. Its September rise was unanimous, and Governor Michele Bullock warned that higher oil prices from the Iran war would push inflation above the bank's earlier forecasts.
beats.happened: Ahead of the decision at 03:30 GMT Tuesday (9:30 PM CT Monday), money markets price roughly four-in-five odds of a rise to 4.85%. Recent quarterly and monthly inflation figures matched or beat forecasts. The bank also publishes its quarterly Statement on Monetary Policy, with updated forecasts, and Bullock speaks an hour later.
beats.means: A rise is mostly expected, so the currency will react more to the message: whether the bank keeps the door open to December, how much it lifts its inflation forecasts, and whether the vote stays unanimous. In September Bullock sounded softer at her news conference than the written statement, which faded the Australian dollar's early gain.
beats.fx: A rise with a firm tone would support the Australian dollar; a hold, a split vote, or a hint that this is the last rise would weigh on it. The New Zealand dollar often moves with it.

impact.why: A likely rate rise keeps Australian rates high, though it is largely priced in.
The kiwi tends to follow the Australian dollar on RBA news.

items.watch: The decision and new forecasts at 03:30 GMT Tuesday, then Bullock's news conference an hour later.

items.headline: Oil prices slide more than 3% as Trump signals more time for Iran diplomacy
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Oil fell more than 3% on Monday, with Brent near $110 a barrel, after reports that President Trump wants to give talks with Iran more time before any new US strikes.

beats.was: Brent crude rose about 15% in October to a six-month high as attacks on Gulf shipping and talk of fresh US strikes on Iran raised fears for supply. Iranian officials have been meeting go-betweens in Qatar about ending the war.
beats.happened: Brent dropped to about $110 and US crude to about $101. Axios reported that Trump told Israel's prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, he wanted diplomacy to run longer before weighing more strikes, and Trump said on Sunday the war would end soon one way or another. Ships were still being hit near the Strait of Hormuz and off Saudi Arabia's Gulf coast over the weekend.
beats.means: The market is pricing a better chance of a deal and a smaller chance of new strikes this week, but the attacks at sea show supply is still at risk. The bank UBS still sees Brent near $110 at year-end.
beats.fx: Cheaper oil helps big energy buyers such as Japan and the euro zone and takes some support from oil exporters such as Canada and Norway.

impact.why: Signs Washington will hold off on new strikes cut the war premium in prices.
Lower oil trims support for Canada's main export.
A cheaper energy bill eases a long-running drag on Japan's trade balance.
The euro zone imports most of its energy, so lower oil helps.

items.watch: Whether the Qatar talks yield a plan to reopen Hormuz, and what Washington says about strikes once Tuesday's vote is over.

items.headline: Oil slips more than 1% as talks continue on ending Iran war
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Oil fell about 1.5% as trading opened in Asia on Monday, with Brent near $112 a barrel, as Iran and Qatar held a third day of talks on ending the war.

beats.was: Brent crude ended October at a six-month high after weeks of attacks on Gulf shipping, and the US has said it may strike Iran again. Qatar is acting as go-between for Washington and Tehran.
beats.happened: Brent fell $1.59 to about $111.84 and US crude to about $102.56 early Monday. Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said the talks in Doha were progressing, and a quiet weekend with no major military escalation took some urgency out of prices; OPEC+ also kept December output targets unchanged.
beats.means: The market is shaving a little of the war premium on hopes of a deal, but it remains nervous that fighting could resume after Tuesday's US midterm elections.
beats.fx: Cheaper oil eases the import bill for Japan and Europe and takes a little support away from oil exporters such as Canada.

impact.why: Hopes for a deal to end the war pulled prices well off last week's highs at the open.
Lower oil trims support for Canada's biggest export.
A smaller energy bill helps Japan, which buys nearly all its oil abroad.

items.watch: Whether the Doha talks produce a plan to reopen Hormuz, and what Washington says about strikes after Tuesday's vote.

items.headline: Tanker hit by two projectiles off Saudi coast as Gulf incidents reach 10 in three days
items.story_title: Hormuz: shipping attacks and the oil supply
items.summary: A tanker was struck by two unidentified projectiles in the northern Gulf off Saudi Arabia early Monday, the tenth reported attack on shipping in the region since Saturday.

beats.was: Since the US-Israeli war on Iran began, ships in and near the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow channel that carries about a fifth of the world's oil, have been hit by mines, drones and missiles. Iran's Revolutionary Guards have claimed several of these attacks.
beats.happened: The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre, which tracks shipping security for the Royal Navy, said a tanker sailing southeast was hit on its side about 72 nautical miles east of Ras Al Khafji, near the Saudi-Kuwaiti border. All crew are safe and no spill was reported; the ship and the attacker were not named.
beats.means: The attacks are no longer limited to the strait itself but reach the northern Gulf, where Saudi and Kuwaiti crude is loaded. That tends to lift insurance and freight costs even while talks to end the war continue in Qatar.
beats.fx: More risk to Gulf shipping supports oil prices, which helps oil exporters like Canada and Norway and hurts big importers such as Japan and the euro zone.

impact.why: A new attack further up the Gulf adds to supply risk, but no damage to oil flows was reported and prices stayed lower on the day.
Japan imports almost all its oil, so pricier shipping through the Gulf is a cost for its economy.

items.watch: Whether anyone claims the attack, and whether tanker traffic out of Saudi and Kuwaiti ports slows.

items.headline: China private factory PMI at 52.0 beats forecasts, output growth fastest since April
items.story_title: China: a slowing economy
items.summary: A private survey of Chinese factories came in at 52.0 for October, better than the 51.6 expected, with output growing at its fastest pace in six months.

beats.was: China's official factory survey, released on Saturday, showed activity shrinking in October (49.3, below the 50 line that splits growth from decline), which had raised worries about Australia's and New Zealand's biggest customer.
beats.happened: The RatingDog survey, compiled by S&P Global and tilted toward exporters, slipped only slightly from 52.1 in September. Output and buying picked up, but export orders grew at their slowest in three months, factories cut selling prices, and business confidence fell to a nine-month low.
beats.means: China's private exporters are holding up better than the official numbers suggest, which eases fears of a sharp slowdown. Falling factory prices still point to weak demand at home and keep pressure on Beijing to add support.
beats.fx: Better Chinese factory activity gives some relief to currencies tied to China's demand, mainly the Australian and New Zealand dollars.

impact.why: A beat from Australia's biggest customer softens Saturday's weak official survey, though the mix inside is soft.
Steadier Chinese factories help demand for New Zealand's exports a little.

items.watch: China's services survey later this week, and whether Beijing's market regulators announce support after meeting banks on Monday.

items.headline: Japan's Katayama says US-Japan FX statement 'alive', warns on disorderly yen moves
items.story_title: Japan: guarding the yen near 160 per dollar
items.summary: Japan's finance minister said Tokyo's currency pact with Washington still stands whatever happens in Tuesday's US midterm elections, and that Japan will step in against wild swings in the yen.

beats.was: The yen has been weak all year and slid close to 160 per dollar, a level where Japan has sold dollars to prop it up before. Japan and the US agreed a joint statement on currencies that accepts action against disorderly moves.
beats.happened: Satsuki Katayama, Japan's finance minister, said on Monday that the joint statement is still in force and that the two governments will stay aligned after the US vote. She would not judge the yen's current level, but said markets are calmer than before and that Japan will act against disorderly or speculative moves.
beats.means: The warning is a reminder that Tokyo is still watching, which puts a soft ceiling on how far the dollar can climb against the yen. But she sounded less urgent than when the yen was near 160, so this is a standing guard, not a sign of action soon.
beats.fx: It mildly supports the yen by keeping the threat of Japanese buying alive, and limits the dollar's room to rise against it.

impact.why: Repeats a known warning; it keeps a floor under the yen but adds no new pressure.
Caps how far the dollar can rise against the yen while the threat of action stands.

items.watch: How fast the dollar moves against the yen around Tuesday's US vote and Friday's jobs report; a quick run back toward 160 is what would bring sharper words or action.

items.headline: Trump Says U.S. and Canada 'Very Close' to Trade Deal, Carney Cites Constructive Talks
items.story_title: US-Canada trade: tariffs and talks
items.summary: President Trump told an Iowa rally on Sunday that the US and Canada are very close to a trade deal that would include the Keystone XL oil pipeline, while Prime Minister Mark Carney said talks will take weeks.

beats.was: The US and Canada have put billions of dollars of tariffs on each other's goods in recent months, hurting Canadian steel and car makers. The Keystone XL pipeline, which would carry Canadian crude to the US, was cancelled in 2021.
beats.happened: Trump said he spoke with Carney by phone on Saturday and that the two sides have outlined a very good deal, with Canada paying to build the pipeline. Carney called the talks constructive but said negotiators will work on a framework over the coming weeks; no terms or tariff cuts were announced.
beats.means: It is the warmest tone in months, two days before the US midterm elections, but nothing is signed and Carney has said before that Canada will not rush into a bad deal.
beats.fx: Lower US tariffs would help Canada's exports and economy, which have stalled, so real progress would support the Canadian dollar; the market will want details first.

impact.why: Talk of a deal that could cut tariffs on Canadian goods helps, but there are no terms yet.

items.watch: Whether either side publishes terms, especially tariff relief on Canadian steel and cars.

items.headline: RBA Rate Hike Looms Amid Global Worries
items.story_title: Reserve Bank of Australia: a fifth rate rise this year?
items.summary: Economists expect the Reserve Bank of Australia to raise its rate on Tuesday, November 3, by a quarter point to 4.85%, and several think it will be the last rise of this run.

beats.was: Australia's central bank has raised its cash rate four times this year, to 4.60%, because inflation has stayed well above its target. Recent price figures came in hotter than expected.
beats.happened: Money markets now give a quarter-point rise a high chance at Tuesday's meeting, which would take the rate to 4.85%, among its highest in nearly two decades. The big Australian banks and several economists say this could be the peak.
beats.means: A rise is largely expected, so the Australian dollar's reaction will hang on what the bank says about the next step. A hint that this is the last rise could take some shine off the currency, and a surprise hold would hit it harder.
beats.fx: A hike with a firm tone would support the Australian dollar; a hold or a clear signal of a pause would weigh on it.

impact.why: An expected rate rise keeps Australian rates high, but it is mostly priced already.
The New Zealand dollar often moves with its neighbour's currency on Australian news.

items.watch: The decision and statement at 2:30 PM Australian east coast time on Tuesday (03:30 GMT), then the governor's news conference.

items.headline: Germany Misses Gas Storage Target as Cold Snap Sets In
items.story_title: Europe's gas: thin reserves going into winter
items.summary: Germany's gas stores were only about 61% full on November 1, short of its 70% goal, just as colder-than-usual weather arrives.

beats.was: Germany sets fill targets for its gas storage so it can get through winter, and European gas prices have roughly tripled this year because the Iran war cut Gulf supplies, topping €100 per megawatt-hour last week for the first time since 2022.
beats.happened: Data from Gas Infrastructure Europe showed German storage at 61% on Friday versus a 70% target, well below the EU average of 75%. The economy ministry admitted the target will be missed but said reserves should last the winter thanks to Norwegian pipelines and LNG terminals. Forecasts show temperatures below normal in Berlin, Frankfurt and Munich.
beats.means: Thin reserves plus a cold, possibly windless spell mean Germany may have to buy more gas at high prices, which raises costs for its factories and keeps energy inflation up.
beats.fx: Pricier energy hurts Europe's trade balance and growth, a weight on the euro, though it also keeps inflation high enough for the European Central Bank to consider raising rates.

impact.why: Low gas stores before a cold spell raise the euro zone's energy bill and the risk to German industry.

items.watch: How cold November turns out and whether European gas prices climb back above €100.

items.headline: Bank of England expected to raise interest rates to 4%
items.story_title: Bank of England's first rate rise since 2023
items.summary: Economists expect the Bank of England to lift its main rate from 3.75% to 4% on Thursday, November 5, its first rise since August 2023.

beats.was: UK inflation has stayed well above the Bank of England's 2% goal, and fuel costs have risen with the Middle East war. The household energy price cap went up 3.6% in October, and a far bigger rise is forecast for January.
beats.happened: Ahead of Thursday's decision, economists at Investec and the ICAEW, the accountants' body, said a quarter-point rise to 4% looks close to certain, framed as a move to stop high prices from becoming the norm.
beats.means: A rise is now the expected outcome, so it would confirm what markets already assume. What matters more is how many of the nine policymakers vote for it and whether the Bank hints at more.
beats.fx: The pound has gained on this expectation. A rise with signals of more could add to it, while a hold or a split vote that sounds reluctant would likely knock it.

impact.why: Higher UK rates support the pound, but the rise is largely priced in already.

items.watch: The vote split and the Bank's guidance on Thursday; a hold would be a real surprise.

items.headline: Two oil tankers explode after hitting mine in Hormuz Strait, IRGC says
items.story_title: Hormuz: shipping attacks and the oil supply
items.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards said two oil tankers hit Iranian sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday, leaving one supertanker on fire, while a UK shipping-security agency reported another tanker struck by an unknown projectile.

beats.was: The Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane that carries about a fifth of the world's oil, has been largely shut since the US-Iran war began in February, and ships trying to pass have been mined, shot at or seized. Several tankers were hit last week.
beats.happened: A spokesman for the Guards' navy told Iranian state TV the two tankers took an unapproved route with their tracking systems off and blamed their owners. Separately, the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre said a tanker was hit by an unknown object earlier on Sunday. None of this has been independently confirmed.
beats.means: Ships keep getting hit even as Iran and the US talk through Qatar, so the few routes still open look riskier and insurance and freight costs stay high.
beats.fx: More damage to Gulf shipping supports oil prices, which helps oil exporters like Canada and hurts big importers such as Japan and the euro zone.

impact.why: Two more tankers hit in the main Gulf oil lane raises the risk that even less crude gets out.
Japan buys almost all its oil abroad, so a higher import bill weighs on the yen.
Canada sells a lot of oil, so Gulf supply scares tend to lift the loonie a little.

items.watch: Whether Monday's oil trading opens higher, and whether the US Navy or shipping agencies confirm the Iranian account.

items.headline: Trump holds call with Netanyahu amid preparations to renew strikes on Iran -- report
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: The US is preparing for possible new strikes on Iran, with Gulf allies reportedly warned they could come as soon as November 4, while talks carry on.

beats.was: The US has not struck Iran since September 1, and talks run through Qatar. Washington has been telling Gulf partners to get ready for action after Tuesday's US midterm elections.
beats.happened: President Donald Trump spoke with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday, The Wall Street Journal reported, and said the US still needs to deal with "one or two sites" in Iran. One report says Gulf allies were warned of strikes as early as November 4. A top Iranian security official said Tehran is debating whether to drop its ban on nuclear weapons if fighting resumes.
beats.means: The risk of the war flaring up again in the coming days has gone up, even as both sides keep talking. Trump still says talks are going fine.
beats.fx: Fresh fighting would likely push oil higher and send money into shelter currencies like the Swiss franc. It would hurt big oil importers such as Japan and the euro zone.

impact.why: Reports of strike preparations raise the odds of new fighting near the main oil sea lane.
War risk tends to draw shelter money into the franc.
The euro zone imports most of its energy, so a jump in oil would weigh on it.

items.watch: Any US decision on strikes after the November 3 midterm elections, and any reply to Iran's two-day reopening offer.
